page.title: Alerts and actions
page.contact: Can't speak? Write a message to show the medical officer →
page.allWithin: All measured indicators are within the general range and personal pattern.
page.noRecords: No records to review. Complete a check-in to track your indicators.
page.togetherExplanation: Indicators that moved away from expected values on the same days. This does not mean one caused the other, and it does not change any alert level.
page.noTogether: No pair of indicators changed together in recent days.

bloodPressure.whyItMatters: Without gravity, body fluids shift toward the head. In eight astronauts, all men, average 24-hour inflight blood pressure was 8 mmHg lower systolic and 9 mmHg lower diastolic than on the ground, with unchanged heart rate. The study does not define a safe range for an individual.
bloodPressure.yellow: Rest for 10 minutes, repeat the measurement, and record it again.
bloodPressure.red: Repeat the measurement, rest, and notify the onboard medical officer.

heartRate.whyItMatters: Microgravity changes circulation and how the heart works.
heartRate.yellow: Rest for 10 minutes, repeat the measurement, and record it again.
heartRate.red: Rest and notify the onboard medical officer.

glucose.whyItMatters: Sentinela includes glucose because the challenge mentions blood sugar, and only selected profiles track it. We found no routine inflight glucose monitoring in the NASA sources reviewed. This does not rule out research or individual indications, or make glucose a measure of adequate nutrition.
glucose.yellow: Record what and when you ate, then measure again while fasting according to the protocol.
glucose.red: Measure again now and notify the onboard medical officer.

temperature.whyItMatters: Spaceflight stress affects the immune response and can reactivate dormant viruses in the body.
temperature.yellow: Measure again in 1 hour and watch for other symptoms.
temperature.red: Notify the onboard medical officer and follow the mission medical protocol.

sleepHours.whyItMatters: The crew sees about 16 sunrises a day on the station, which disrupts the body clock. Too little sleep reduces alertness and performance.
sleepHours.yellow: Protect today's rest period and adjust cabin lighting according to protocol.
sleepHours.red: Notify the onboard medical officer and avoid critical tasks until rested.

mood.whyItMatters: Isolation, confinement, and distance from Earth can weigh on mood during a mission. The trend matters, not one isolated day.
mood.yellow: Use the journal and keep planned contact with the team and family.
mood.red: Talk with the onboard medical officer or mission psychological support.

stress.whyItMatters: Isolation, confinement, and distance from Earth can increase stress during a mission. In a study of 24 astronauts on the station, sleeping 6 hours or less occurred alongside higher stress.
stress.yellow: Set aside time to rest today and talk with a crewmate or family at the next contact.
stress.red: Talk with the onboard medical officer or mission psychological support.

workload.whyItMatters: Work overload is one factor in NASA's risk of poor sleep and irregular schedules. Heavy workload over several days can reduce alertness and performance.
workload.yellow: Ask the commander whether tasks can be redistributed, and protect tonight's sleep period.
workload.red: Notify the commander and onboard medical officer to review the work schedule.

exerciseMinutes.whyItMatters: Microgravity affects bones and muscles. NASA reports an average loss of 1% to 1.5% per month in weight-bearing bones in 4- to 6-month missions; this is not an individual prediction. Exercise is part of the mission countermeasures.
exerciseMinutes.yellow: Record the type of exercise and make up the session according to your individual plan.
exerciseMinutes.red: Talk with the onboard medical officer before resuming or changing your exercise plan.

radiationDose.whyItMatters: Space radiation increases lifetime cancer risk. Today's dose is compared with your own mission history.
radiationDose.yellow: Spend more time in better-shielded areas and follow the mission radiation protocol.
radiationDose.red: Go to the shelter area and notify the onboard medical officer.

vision.whyItMatters: On long ISS missions, about 70% show early signs detectable by optical coherence tomography. A 2023 NASA brief reports optic disc edema in 16% during or after long missions; the criteria differ. This self-report does not diagnose SANS or replace an eye examination.
vision.yellow: Record what changed and repeat the self-test tomorrow at the same time.
vision.red: Notify the onboard medical officer and request an eye evaluation.

medication.whyItMatters: There is no rapid resupply far from Earth, and the body changes during flight, which can affect how medication works. Knowing whether each scheduled dose was taken helps the onboard medical officer assess treatment.
medication.yellow: Check your medication plan to see whether you can still take today's dose. If unsure, ask the medical officer before taking two doses together.

symptoms.whyItMatters: Far from Earth, recording a symptom early gives the crew time to act with onboard resources.
symptoms.yellow: Note when it started and how it changes, then record it again tomorrow.
symptoms.red: Notify the onboard medical officer now.

co2High.yellow: Because cabin CO2 is above 3 mmHg, check cabin ventilation and tell the medical officer about the symptom.
co2High.red: Because cabin CO2 is above 3 mmHg, check cabin ventilation and notify the medical officer now.

reactionTime.whyItMatters: A study of 24 astronauts found an association between sleeping 6 hours or less and slower reactions. This app's test is a demo, not equivalent to the validated Reaction Self Test protocol, and does not diagnose fatigue.
reactionTime.yellow: Prioritize your next sleep period and retake the test tomorrow. If it stays slower, talk with the medical officer about fatigue countermeasures.

resistanceMinutes.whyItMatters: Resistance training protects bones the most in flight. A NASA study on the station showed that resistance training reduces bone loss, but does not prevent it on its own.
resistanceMinutes.yellow: Make up the resistance training session according to your individual plan.
resistanceMinutes.red: Talk with the onboard medical officer before resuming or changing your exercise plan.

bodyMassKg.whyItMatters: Body mass is an indicator of nutrition during flight. The comparison is with this mission's starting value, not a universal range.
bodyMassKg.yellow: Review food, hydration, and the plan with the medical officer.
bodyMassKg.red: Notify the medical officer now to review nutrition and the mission plan.

radiationDose.station: The station is inside the magnetosphere, which blocks much of the radiation.
radiationDose.transit: Outside the magnetosphere, exposure is higher. Follow the mission shelter protocol.
radiationDose.moon: The Moon is outside the magnetosphere. Use the habitat's better-shielded areas.
radiationDose.mars: Outside the magnetosphere, with ground response times of up to 20 minutes.
